sources.title: Archived Helen Clark biography: birth, parliamentary constituencies and ministerial dates
sources.findings: Read the New Zealand Parliament archived biography. It gives 26 February 1950 in Hamilton, ministerial dates, 8 August 1989–2 November 1990 as deputy prime minister, and 10 December 1999–19 November 2008 as prime minister. Its constituency record distinguishes Mount Albert before/after Owairaka in 1996–1999; do not repeat simplified claims of one unchanged constituency throughout 1981–2009. The party-activities section lists a 1996 Labour-leader start inconsistent with its own 1 December 1993 opposition-leader record and official NZ History; use corroborated 1993, not the isolated 1996 entry. It lists final parliamentary service through 18 April 2009 while raw summaries use 17 April; the dossier uses April only.

sources.title: Personal biography: Hamilton birth, Te Pahu upbringing and political career
sources.findings: Read the personal biography’s childhood and early-career sections. It distinguishes Hamilton hospital birthplace from the Te Pahu farm where she grew up; 1968 is enrolment, not graduation. It corroborates study/teaching, 1987–1990 ministerial experience, 1989–1990 deputy premiership and 1993 party leadership. Its uninterrupted Mount Albert shorthand is refined by Parliament’s constituency record. Promotional economic assessments are not treated as independently measured personal achievements or proof that policy was uncontested.

sources.title: 2015–2016 University Profile: BA 1971, MA 1974 and honorary LLD 2010
sources.findings: Read the alumni paragraph of the University of Auckland 2015–2016 Profile. It explicitly records BA 1971, MA 1974 and LLD (Honorary) 2010. The honorary law degree is not an earned research doctorate, and its then-current UNDP description is historical. No claim is made to have audited academic transcripts or the entire PDF. The file’s later indexing/upload date is not the degree or publication period.

sources.publisher: Manatū Taonga, Ministry for Culture and Heritage
sources.title: Helen Clark: second woman prime minister, Labour leadership and domestic reforms
sources.findings: Read the NZ History biography passages. They distinguish Jenny Shipley as the first woman prime minister from Clark as the first woman to take office following an election victory, and corroborate the three consecutive Labour election victories and 1993 leadership transition. A prime minister is not directly elected in a separate nationwide presidential-style election. The source describes policy moderation rather than wholesale reversal of Rogernomics, union/civil-rights reforms and a new Supreme Court. The dossier does not assign every economic outcome to Clark alone.

sources.title: Past administrators: Helen Clark’s April 2009–April 2017 tenure
sources.findings: Read the Helen Clark section of UNDP’s past-administrators page. It explicitly gives April 2009–April 2017 and first female administrator, with concurrent chairmanship of the UN Development Group. Her UNDP role is neither secretary-general nor a current 2026 appointment. Other administrators’ biographies on the same page, especially their education and awards, were not transferred to her. No unsupported exact April start/end day or independent transparency-ranking result is added.

sources.title: 9 July 2020: independent pandemic evaluation co-chaired by Clark and Sirleaf
sources.findings: Read WHO’s 9 July 2020 announcement of the independent evaluation. Clark and Ellen Johnson Sirleaf are co-chairs, selected following consultation and a World Health Assembly mandate; they choose the other members and secretariat. This is an independent evaluation, not appointment as WHO director-general. The Nobel Peace Prize reference belongs to Sirleaf, not Clark. The announcement’s future reporting timetable is not itself proof the eventual report was delivered; the May 2021 presentation separately establishes that event.

sources.publisher: Independent Panel for Pandemic Preparedness and Response
sources.title: 12 May 2021 presentation: evaluation findings and preparedness reform recommendations
sources.findings: Read the panel’s presentation header, selected findings and recommendation passages, including the named speakers. The presentation occurred on 12 May 2021, while the web page is dated 19 May. It summarises assessment of early warning/response and calls for stronger WHO authority, financing, vaccine equity and preparedness. Recommendations are collective proposals, not proof of a new binding treaty or full implementation. Sirleaf’s passages are not automatically Clark’s personal quotations. No claim to have reviewed the complete main report, all evidence annexes or video recording is made; historical casualty/dose figures and proposed financing amounts were not carried forward as current totals.

sources.title: 23 July 2021 announcement: Clark elected one of three institute presidents
sources.findings: Read Chatham House’s 23 July 2021 election announcement, updated 17 August. It names Clark as replacing John Major and joining two other serving presidents; that is institute governance rather than director/CEO or sole president. It independently identifies her as the eighth UNDP administrator and first woman. The timeline dates the announcement, not an independently verified installation ceremony. Current Chatham presidency is not asserted as the dossier’s main 2026 office because the latest role-filtered roster omits her despite 2025 and July 2026 materials naming her.

sources.publisher: Manatū Taonga, Ministry for Culture and Heritage
sources.title: Treaty timeline: 2004 foreshore and seabed legislation and Māori opposition
sources.findings: Read the official Treaty timeline’s 2004 section. It records passage of the Foreshore and Seabed Act in November, Crown ownership/public-access provisions, widespread Māori opposition regarding customary rights and Treaty obligations, the May hīkoi and formation of the Māori Party. The public text attributes the rights/Treaty criticism to Māori opponents; it is not a claimed judicial conviction of Clark or a declaration that the law remains in force. No original tribunal report or full contemporaneous legislative debate was reviewed.

sources.title: Indexed statutory status: Foreshore and Seabed Act 2004 repealed on 1 April 2011
sources.findings: Read the official New Zealand Legislation indexed status text: the 2004 Act was repealed on 1 April 2011 by section 5 of the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act 2011. Opening the full statute returned HTTP 403. The repeal status is used narrowly, not to claim review of the full legal text, all later amendments or current individual customary-title litigation.

sources.title: 8 November 2026 interview: Clark calls for review of New Zealand electoral rules
sources.findings: Read the AAP-bylined 1News report at its 8 November 2026 URL, especially the direct-interview passage. Clark calls for review of electoral, enrolment and campaign-funding rules; this is recent interview evidence. Her view that the election might be flawed is not a final judicial or observer ruling. The report describes preliminary results and additional ballots due on 27 November, which remains future at this cutoff; no final seat count, coalition outcome or invalidation is asserted. No linked video or social-media account was independently examined.

sources.title: 6 October 2025 appointment: Clark to succeed Barroso as board chair from January 2026
sources.findings: Read Gavi’s 6 October 2025 appointment release. It distinguishes selection in October 2025 from the January 2026 start, succession to José Manuel Barroso and Sania Nishtar’s separate CEO position. The announcement alone would be prospective; current board membership and the January biography establish the role was taken up. Its description of future strategic priorities and funding ambitions is not a verified record of already delivered benefits.

sources.title: Board roster updated 5 November 2026: Helen Clark as chair, Sania Nishtar as CEO
sources.findings: Read Gavi’s board-members table, explicitly updated 5 November 2026. It lists Helen Clark in the independent individual/chair seat, with term scheduled to end 31 December 2027, and Sania Nishtar as CEO. The board roster supports the current chairmanship; a scheduled term end is not a guarantee of future service. It is a governance record rather than independent proof of a particular in-person appearance.

sources.title: January 2026 board-chair biography and former UNDP leadership
sources.findings: Read Gavi’s Helen Clark board-chair biography, updated 6 January 2026. It confirms January commencement and April 2009–April 2017 UNDP service. Its list of other boards and rankings was not adopted wholesale as independently refreshed current facts. Honorary or advocacy positions are not conflated with executive management; no claim is made that UNDP’s performance was caused by one person alone.

sources.title: 2 July 2026 board decisions: strategy targets, financial constraints and governance appointments
sources.findings: Read selected sections of Gavi’s 2 July 2026 board-meeting release. It identifies Clark as chair and Nishtar as CEO, differentiates decisions for 2026–2030 from the previous 2021–2025 period, and notes financing constraints and targets. Target vaccinations, mortality reduction, economic benefits and approved financing access are not already delivered outcomes or disbursed funds. Earlier-period achievements are not assigned to Clark’s chairmanship beginning in 2026. Future effective dates for other board appointments were not confused with the announcement date.
